clinicalPearls: Gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour that causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome through unregulated hypergastrinaemia and gastric acid hypersecretion

Most arise within the gastrinoma triangle, bounded by the junction of the cystic and common bile ducts, the junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum, and the junction of the pancreatic neck and body
Duodenal primaries are now recognised as more common than pancreatic; they are often small and multiple, whereas pancreatic gastrinomas tend to be larger with higher metastatic potential
Approximately 20 to 30 per cent occur within MEN1, typically as multifocal duodenal tumours that require an individualised surgical approach
Malignant behaviour is common, with spread to regional lymph nodes and liver; hepatic metastases are the principal determinant of survival
Gastrinomas strongly express somatostatin receptors, so DOTATATE PET is highly sensitive for localisation and staging
Fasting serum gastrin must be interpreted with concurrent gastric pH and off proton pump inhibitors where safe, since acid suppression itself raises gastrin
Curative resection is achievable for localised sporadic disease, whereas multifocal duodenal MEN1 tumours make cure less likely and management is tailored
reference.pathophysiology: Gastrinoma is a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour that autonomously secretes gastrin. Persistent hypergastrinaemia stimulates enterochromaffin-like and parietal cells, driving parietal cell hyperplasia and marked gastric acid hypersecretion. The resulting hyperchlorhydria produces peptic ulceration that is often multiple, distally located or refractory, together with gastro-oesophageal reflux and secretory diarrhoea from acid injury to the small bowel and inactivation of pancreatic enzymes. Tumours arise from gastrin-producing cells of the duodenum or pancreas; in MEN1 biallelic loss of menin underlies the characteristic multifocal duodenal tumours. Malignant potential relates to size, location (pancreatic more than duodenal) and grade, with the liver the principal site of metastasis.
additionalDifferentials: Proton pump inhibitor-induced hypergastrinaemia, the commonest cause of a raised gastrin
Atrophic gastritis or pernicious anaemia with achlorhydria-driven hypergastrinaemia
Retained gastric antrum syndrome after previous gastric surgery
Renal impairment or gastric outlet obstruction raising gastrin
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum gastrin, off acid suppression where safe, with concurrent gastric pH or acid output
Secretin stimulation test showing a paradoxical rise in gastrin to confirm gastrinoma
Chromogranin A as a general neuroendocrine tumour marker
Somatostatin receptor PET/CT (DOTATATE) for localisation and staging
Endoscopic ultrasound and multiphase CT or MRI, with attention to the duodenum and gastrinoma triangle
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy documenting ulcers, prominent gastric folds and duodenal lesions
MEN1 genetic testing with serum calcium, PTH and prolactin
redFlags: Complicated peptic ulcer disease with haemorrhage, perforation or gastric outlet obstruction
Multiple or distal duodenal or jejunal ulcers, or ulcers refractory to standard therapy
Peptic ulceration accompanied by chronic diarrhoea and weight loss
Features of MEN1 prompting family screening
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely determined by the presence and extent of hepatic metastases and by tumour grade: localised gastrinoma has favourable long-term survival after resection, whereas diffuse hepatic metastatic disease carries a considerably poorer outlook despite effective acid control.
pitfalls: Measuring gastrin while the patient is taking a proton pump inhibitor, producing misleading elevation
Attributing recurrent ulcers to Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs and missing an underlying gastrinoma
Searching only the pancreas and overlooking small duodenal primaries
Stopping acid suppression abruptly for testing without safeguards, risking severe ulcer complications
Failing to screen for MEN1, which alters surgical strategy and family management
references: ENETS Consensus Guidelines for gastrinoma and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
management: Control gastric acid hypersecretion with high-dose proton-pump inhibitor therapy, the cornerstone of symptom control
Resect localised sporadic tumours, which can be curative, after localising within the gastrinoma triangle using endoscopic ultrasound, multiphase cross-sectional imaging and DOTATATE PET
Use somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide for hormonal and antiproliferative control in advanced disease
For metastatic disease, employ peptide receptor radionuclide therapy with lutetium-DOTATATE, targeted agents such as everolimus or sunitinib, systemic chemotherapy and liver-directed therapy
Screen for MEN1, including hyperparathyroidism and pituitary disease, and take an individualised surgical approach to multifocal duodenal tumours
Undertake surveillance imaging with chromogranin A and gastrin monitoring for recurrence and hepatic metastasis
Offer genetic counselling and family screening where MEN1 is identified
